reading.body:
Banking is where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade: Fed SR 11-7 model risk rules already cover credit and AML models, and generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

The pattern is that banking's AI oversight is older than the current generative wave. Credit and AML models have operated under SR 11-7 since 2011, so the sector enters the generative era with pre-existing validation, documentation, and model risk requirements. Treasury's report frames the supervisory conversation, and the Evident AI Banking Index provides a public scoreboard across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

For AI specifically, this means generative deployments in service and compliance inherit a governance burden that most other industries lack. A bank cannot launch a customer-facing chatbot or compliance assistant without treating it as a model under SR 11-7, which slows deployment but also reduces the chance of unmanaged failures. The data does not show scale. It contains no figures on compute demand or power consumption for banking AI, and no adoption rates or model sizes. Governance is the constraint the data documents, not infrastructure.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in finance and insurance, NAICS 52, at 40.1% in the latest reading, down from 41.0% in the prior period. The question asked is whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and the survey first asked it in September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in the material, and it covers the whole finance and insurance sector rather than banking alone.

What banks actually do with AI is described by Evident Insights, whose Evident AI Index benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services and scores the world's largest banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics covering talent, innovation, leadership and transparency. Evident describes the index as the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard, launched in January 2023, and says several of the world's biggest banks have quietly become AI-powered behemoths while tech companies took the spotlight. It also runs a LATAM edition, where Nubank ranked first in the 2026 index, and a separate index for insurance. On this site, the Financial Models section catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub with licence, downloads and release date, refreshed daily, tracking models tuned for financial text.

The supervisory backdrop predates the current wave. The Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011 and listed in the Fed's 2011 supervisory letters index, already governs credit and AML models, which means banking is the sector where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade. The sourced points describe fraud detection and credit models as decades old, with generative AI in service and compliance as the new frontier, all of it under that same model risk supervision.

The Treasury's report on AI in financial services, covering uses, opportunities and risks, frames the US supervisory conversation, according to the sourced points. The excerpt harvested from the Treasury page itself concerns OFAC sanctions on a gold smuggling and money laundering network, so it does not supply detail on the AI report's contents. The excerpt from the Federal Reserve page likewise shows only the index entry for a 2011 letter on dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries, not the text of SR 11-7.

On money and vendors, the material is thin. Evident notes that AI is breathing new life into Wall Street's tech hiring scene while landing a software job in finance is harder than in recent years, and that its briefing has over 15,000 subscribers across banking, tech, consulting, academia and government. No source here reports ROI figures, deployment spending or vendor market shares, so nothing can be said about where money concentrates beyond that.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few cautious takeaways. Adoption across finance and insurance is real but not universal at 40.1%, and it slipped slightly from 41.0%. Governance is not a blank slate, since SR 11-7 has applied to models in this sector since 2011. Public benchmarking exists through the Evident AI Index, and open financial models are catalogued on this site. The sources do not report ROI evidence, specific risk incidents or detailed regulatory requirements, so those questions remain open on this material.

https://evidentinsights.com/.brief: Evident Insights describes itself as an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption in financial services, aiming to help sector leaders with AI-related decisions, investments and strategic choices. It publishes an AI Index for Banks, including a LATAM edition, and an AI Index for Insurance, with 2026 results discussed in roundtables and reports. Nubank is cited as ranking first in the 2026 Evident AI Index for Banks - LATAM Edition, and its representatives joined Evident to discuss how its digital-native foundations relate to AI advantage. The company also runs an invitation-only annual AI Symposium for senior finance AI leaders and a Banking Brief newsletter that it says has over 15,000 subscribers. Evident states that since the index launched in January 2023 it has drawn debate and press coverage, with CEO Alexandra Mousavizadeh commenting regularly on global AI trends.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each model's licence, download count and release date, and is refreshed daily. It states that the data comes from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page was last verified on 2026-10-07 and carries a suggested citation. It also notes that the site's search covers the full text of all its published pages, which are rebuilt daily from primary sources.
